justification: A dies on the tester's own specification, "It reports two numbers - how sharply the surface stops the foot, and how far the foot slides before it stops", which is exactly the second number A denies he recorded. B dies on "a weighted steel foot on a rail, released from a fixed height", where both "on a rail" and "from a fixed height" refute a hand release with a varying drop. D is the strongest option in the item and is a clean polarity flip of the quoted sentence "The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is still wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test", which ranks his within-school seasonal gap above the between-arena gap, the reverse of what D asserts.

A is reversed by "the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top", so the wax was better, not worn off, low down. B is refuted by "the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them", so the sand had not broken down. C is refuted twice over by "Eighty millimetres of it had not been turned since the day it was laid, and under nine years of hoofprints it had gone firm enough to lean a spade on" - below the tines the bed was firm, not loose, and the text attributes that firming to hoofprints rather than exempting the depth from them.

A is refuted by "The waxed ones move, whatever their age", which severs age from the effect, and by "some of them older than this one", so the comparison arenas are not systematically newer. C is refuted by the naming of those schools as "laid on plain sand and fibre" - they do carry fibre - and by the mechanism paragraph, where the thing that stiffens in the cold is the coating ("Below about six degrees the coating is stiff"), not the fibre. D is refuted by "He has the same pair of grids from a hundred and forty other arenas" and by the naming of "the morning grid and the afternoon grid" for those very schools, so the reading hours are the same and the protocol would catch any change.

B is refuted by "he says he would argue it from the veterinary literature rather than from his own figures", which is the explicit denial that the footing-change association rests on his readings. C is refuted by "it is worth more than they are" and by "the care is the most useful thing about him", and by the closing paragraph in which the yard acts on exactly this work (heaters, tines at eighty). D is the softest kill in the item and dies by reversal rather than by one sentence: the riders' January/July report is the one claim the readings corroborate ("Both numbers moved, and they moved together"), the displaced explanations are the yard's (machine, mix, man on the tractor), and the doubt the writer endorses is aimed at the reach of the figures ("A number for it is more than these readings will carry") - so her asymmetry runs the opposite way to D, which is additionally non-responsive to the stem.

A is refuted by "the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them, and the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top" plus "whatever their age" - the bed is neither degraded nor near the end of its life, and cold makes it stiff, not damaged. B is the item's strongest distractor because it over-extends the yard's own remedy, but it dies on two spans: the heaters set only a floor ("to have the school above eight degrees before the first lesson"), while July's fault is the top end ("Above about twenty-five it goes slack ... the floor gets deep"), and the February afternoon already read eighteen with no heating at all, so warming removes one end of the range and cannot equalise February with July. D is a verbatim reversal of "The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is", and the hedge "may" does not rescue a reversal (law 11).

A "Hence" asserts that the unanimous ending follows from the unanimous start, which the text denies: "again there has been no signal" marks recurrence rather than consequence, and the next paragraph makes the ending a separate and harder coordination problem ("Ending is the harder half"). B "Rather" is corrective and needs a preceding claim to displace, but the two sentences stand in parallel, again marked by "again there has been no signal". D "Elsewhere" is locational, while the whole paragraph is one room ("the school hall", "two hundred people") and the contrast being drawn is temporal, start against end.

B "cut in" is a live phrasal verb but means to interrupt or interject, whereas the gap needs participation in something already begun, as the next sentence confirms: "the second pair of hands matters more than the first: it turns a private view into a public event". C "fall in" is the closest call in the cloze and is the batch's one purely collocational kill: bare "fall in" is drill formation and needs "with" or "behind" to mean going along with someone, so it does not carry the sense of joining an activity in progress that "join in" carries unaided. D "break in" means to intrude or interrupt, the wrong sense and the wrong polarity, since what is feared is the room's failure to participate, not its intrusion.

A "transaction" fails on the complement and the sense: a transaction is between parties or in something, not "about how long is decent", and it names an exchange rather than the working-out that "the coming-down" is. C "bargain" names the result rather than the process and is struck or driven, not "conducted", while the paragraph describes an unresolved working-out under time pressure ("the sound comes down faster than it went up"). D "settlement" fails the same way as C, naming the outcome and refusing "conducted at speed and without words"; note that all three distractors die on the single axis of process-noun-taking-conducted, so the gap discriminates on one fact.

A "grudging" destroys the concessive: grudging and short agree, so "Although ... it is not permitted to run long" would have no contrast to mark. B "outspoken" is the nearest competitor because the passage runs a speech metaphor for clapping ("an opinion nobody asked for", "a private view"), but it names frankness of speech rather than warmth, so "what a hall gives" cannot be outspoken and it supplies no contrast with brevity. C "muted" fails on the same polarity test as A; the gap's concessive requires the positive term, and the key is the only unambiguously positive option in the set.

A "narrowly" has no collocation with "give one" and is a margin adverb (narrowly won, narrowly avoided), so it fails on sense and selection alike. C "instinctively" is collocationally perfect and draws cover from the passage's celebration of the automatic ("A hall organises itself in about a fifth of a second"), but it is refuted by the frame of this very sentence, "A room asked for a big hand" - the applause is requested, not spontaneous - and by "everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder got". D "generously" is refuted by that same closing clause, since the requested hand is audibly the lesser sound and the paragraph is the failure case ("The mechanism shows itself when it slips").

A is the batch's cleanest right-material-wrong-cause trap - the reject halving is verbatim true ("rejects are down by about half") - but it dies on "The loop runs at the speed it always has. What changed is the bins". B dies on "Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning", so the pink is a post-centrifugation finding, not a ward-side one. C dies on the flat reversal "Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down".

A dies on "The neighbour's attorney enclosed a tracing of the railway company's deposited plan" - the plan entered from the other side, so A is verbatim material attached to the wrong attorney. B dies on the date arithmetic: "both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839" against a claim of November 1845 is six years, not a generation (and 1839 to the joint laying of 1851 is twelve). C dies on "The scheme was given up in the autumn of 1846, and no land was taken".

B is a verbatim polarity flip and dies on “Ett svepskäl är det inte”, reinforced by “jag skriver under på den”. C is refuted by “Fler särskilda kvällar begär jag inte” - she raises the very escalation C proposes (“Fyra kan bli sex och sedan åtta”) only to reject it - and by “Att ensemblen vänjer sig vid remsan kan jag inte lova”, which refuses to make habituation the condition. D is refuted by “Om lilla scenen kan bära samma sak vet jag inte” and “något förslag för den scenen har jag inte”, and by the proposal being for the main stage from next season; D recombines “ett helt spelår” from an unrelated sentence.

A is refuted by “Salongen har en hörselslinga, och den gör vad den ska”, written of the current autumn. B is refuted by “Jag har suttit på rad tre och på rad sexton och hört lika bra på båda”. C is refuted by “Slingans symbol finns längst ned på varje uppslag i programbladet och har gjort det i alla år”, and is the strongest here because it transfers the captioning service's marginality - the squeezed-in row of the title - onto the loop.

B is refuted by “mot det hjälper varken broddar eller lättare lass” - “broddar” is verbatim in the passage but fixed to the opposite conclusion - and by the horse having been kept in the stable at all. C is refuted by “Lassen gick på kälke i stället, och kälken drogs till fots” and by “Skidor dög till att ta sig fram med, men inte till att dra med”, a sentence that exists precisely to kill that reading. D is refuted by “Skaren är inte hal om morgonen. Den är sträv som fint grus under sulan, och blank blir den först fram på dagen” - the right words attached to the wrong hour.

A is refuted by “Var gård körde för sig, och sällan väntade någon in grannen”. C is refuted by “Man ger sig i väg vid fyra ... och vid tio är det över” and by “Bärigheten varar några timmar” - a morning window repeated over many mornings (“fyra morgnar på hela vintern”, “räckte i tre veckor”), not one long night. D is the exact inverse of the mechanism and dies on “Vintrar då kylan håller i sig utan avbrott lämnar snön lös hela vägen ner, för den hinner inte bli våt”.
